Tract agrees that load and generation interconnection requests should have the option to undertake netted study situations, but it should not be required.

letters.desc: TAPS supports an SSR/RMR-type study before any generator partially suspends to serve a co-located large load, and argues the study must include resource adequacy and capacity market analysis. Results should be made public to allow regulators and stakeholders to assess impacts.
quotes: TAPS agrees that there should be an SSR/RMR-type study for existing generating facilities that seek to enter a partial suspension to service a Qualifying Large Load at the same location. Such a study is important to ensure reliability of the transmission system.

the unique size and accelerated timing of new large data center loads, coupled with existing resource adequacy challenges (given retirements of generation and generation interconnection queue backlogs creating barriers to their timely replacement), make it vital to understand the resource adequacy and capacity market implications of taking generation that now serves regional load and instead sequestering it to exclusively serve a co-located large data center load.

letters.desc: VEIR sees self-build flexibility as creating space for co-location of load and generation, and cites ANOPR Principles 8 and 9 as providing useful room for innovative technical approaches.
quotes: VEIR is encouraged by the principles outlined in the ANOPR and particularly supports Principles 8 and 9, which highlight the value of allowing large load developers to build or fund their own network upgrades. We believe this flexibility can accelerate deployment and create space for innovative technical approaches to interconnection and co-location of load and generation.

letters.desc: The VSCC supports fast-tracking co-located load and generation but says this should be done by flagging co-located projects for the RTO to move to an accelerated generator interconnection process, rather than creating a separate large load queue at the RTO. PJM's Reliability Resource Initiative is cited as an approved model.
quotes: The Commission should enable the accelerated interconnection of large loads that are willing to bring their own generation or to be co-located with generation by creating a fast-track generator interconnection queue for those verified generation resources, such as PJM's existing Commission-approved Reliability Resource Initiative.

the interconnection study of large loads that agree to be curtailable and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable and dispatchable should be expedited. Many states, including Virginia, are currently addressing data center load flexibility, and a cooperative approach in this proceeding would allow these efforts to proceed.

letters.desc: The VSCC supports a voluntary fast-track queue for co-located loads, where hybrid facilities pairing load with generation or storage receive a streamlined interconnection study process in exchange for installing system protection facilities.
quotes: FERC should establish the criteria for eligible large load interconnections to voluntarily enter a separate queue when they can demonstrate system impact mitigation through co-location, curtailment, or a combination of both.

letters.desc: Vistra urges the Commission to prioritize co-location rulemaking as the fastest path to actionable reform, noting that the necessary study process already covers existing-generator co-location while new generator co-location requires new tariff language. Net load should be the basis for transmission charges in co-located arrangements.
quotes: co-location arrangements involving new generators will require new tariff language to effectuate the coordinated and expedited study of new load co-located with new generation.  The Commission should prioritize doing so as soon as possible because it 'will allow for efficient siting of loads and generating facilities and thereby minimize the need for costly network upgrades.'
in keeping with the cost causation principle, transmission service charges should be based on actual use of the transmission system, as measured by the facility's net load.

letters.desc: Vistra argues that co-location is the fastest and most efficient path to meeting large load demand. It urges FERC to first clarify that existing rules already permit co-location with existing generators, then develop new pro forma tariff language for co-located new load and new generation, before turning to standalone load interconnection.
quotes: the Commission should issue—as soon as possible—unequivocal determinations (either in Docket No. EL25-49 et al., other pending docket(s), or in this docket) that provide immediate clarity on how existing rules should be applied while the Commission works to implement reforms in this proceeding.
The co-location of large loads with existing generation resources is permissible under existing rules, including generator modification rules, and the 'necessary study' process.

the Commission must not allow parties that seek to delay new large load interconnections to use this important proceeding to freeze the industry and prevent the rapid development of digital infrastructure needed to win the AI race.

It would be remarkably inefficient—and unduly discriminatory—to inadvertently incentivize the retirement of existing generation at exactly the wrong moment by creating barriers to the co-location of new loads with existing generating facilities.

the Commission should make clear that co-location arrangements involving new load and new generation should minimize the need for network upgrades, minimize line losses, and create efficiencies in equipment, land use, permitting, and siting.

Providing transmission service to co-located facilities based on their actual use of the transmission system will incentivize more new large loads to interconnect via co-location, which is undoubtedly the large load interconnection model most likely to fulfill speed-to-power needs while minimizing strain on the grid.

Vistra supports enabling transmission providers to identify and impose requirements to ensure that co-located facilities inject and withdraw according to their rights, as well as other measures necessary to ensure reliable operation of the transmission system.

letters.desc: The filers treat co-location as a concept that should extend beyond the facility fence line, so capacity distributed across the relevant geographic area qualifies for the same treatment as physically co-located resources.
quotes: new capacity supporting large loads need not be physically co-located at the facility, but can be distributed across the geographic area within which the new load will impact system constraints, provided that the system operator has the requisite level of control to integrate the facility into operations and system planning.

letters.desc: AES supports co-location as a tool to accelerate clean energy deployment but wants rules that allow flexible configurations, avoid physical islanding mandates, treat new and existing generation differently, and do not penalize storage or other innovative resources.
quotes: any incentives should be technology neutral and should not disincentivize other activities that support the grid, such as the development of energy storage or the adoption of innovative technologies.
these incentives should not unduly harm other customers on the system, whether through cost-shifting, or otherwise.
Commission should explore other incentives without the need for physical limitations that effectively island large quantities of new generation.
Financial mechanisms to encourage certain behavior or account for deviations, without the need for potentially costly additional system protection equipment, should also be considered.
AES believes that the Commission should distinguish between co-location of loads with new versus existing generation, as the impacts to existing customers will differ.

AES believes that the system operator should be required to study that generation as a retirement if it is going to be effectively taken behind-the-meter in a manner that removes the energy and capacity benefits from the market.

letters.desc: Alliant Energy is cautiously open to co-located generation and load sharing an interconnection point but insists the Commission require bidirectional flow controls, separate metering, relay schemes, and full NERC compliance. It warns that assuming load and generation offset each other jeopardizes reliability when generation is absent.
quotes: it is critical for the Commission to recognize that simply assuming generation and load offset each other is insufficient and could jeopardize reliability, affordability, and customer interests.

Netting assumes that load and generation at the same point of interconnection can offset one another for transmission planning purposes, but this oversimplification ignores critical operational realities.
the Commission should adopt a gross load approach for both, allowing exceptions only if supported by the utility and approved by the state regulator.
Alliant Energy cautions that netting for ancillary services would understate system obligations, leading to insufficient reserves, jeopardizing reliability, and increasing costs for other customers.

letters.desc: ATC agrees that co-locating load and generation can reduce upgrade needs, but argues current MISO processes already coordinate joint siting. ATC's key condition is process-matching: if the co-located generation can fail independently, the full load must be studied and the load must bear the cost of full network service.
quotes: ATC recommends that the Commission require 'process-matching' when considering how to study hybrid facilities.

If hybrid facilities are not process-matched and the load exceeds studied levels, the transmission system becomes the 'backstop,' and other customers subsidize that excess use through shared costs and reliability impacts.

letters.desc: DCC supports streamlined pathways for hybrid co-located facilities while insisting that stand-alone load must retain access to competitive wholesale markets and that generation pairing remain voluntary, not mandatory.
quotes: DCC urged the Commission to act on the "complete record on co-location issues in PJM" to "deliver immediate clarity."
DCC advocated for studying new load and new generation together to capture system benefits.

Resolving this issue in the existing dockets, and extending principles nationally through this rulemaking, is the most direct way to unlock the significant system benefits that hybrid configurations offer and to provide the certainty developers require.
a durable framework "must allow load to interconnect efficiently, whether or not that load is paired with on-site supply."
pairing of load with generation must remain a voluntary incentive, not a requirement, to avoid unjust and unreasonable discrimination.
Any new interconnection framework must preserve the ability of load to rely on these "competitive markets whose design the Commission has spent more than two decades refining."

letters.desc: ECA sees co-location as a useful tool that can reduce delivery infrastructure costs, but warns that withdrawing existing generation from the market tightens supply and raises prices for other customers. ECA asks the Commission to require market and consumer impact studies beyond reliability-only analyses.
quotes: Co-location arrangements can be a valuable tool for large loads seeking to develop new power supplies or obtain enhanced reliability, and when structured appropriately, help protect existing customers from cost shifts or stranded cost risks by reducing the amount of delivery infrastructure that must be developed to serve large loads. However, co-location with existing generation comes with potential reliability and customer cost impacts for other customers, as taking that generation out of the market can tighten supply and raise prices.

letters.desc: Exelon endorses behind-the-meter or co-located generation models where large loads bring their own dedicated generation, but conditions that support on ensuring full transmission cost responsibility for hybrid facilities.
quotes: Exelon supports generator interconnection reforms that recognize the value in 'bring your own generation' ('BYOG') approaches, in which generation dedicated to serve specific large load customers comes online with financial support and commitments from those customers.
treatments of hybrid configurations need to recognize that associated generators and loads fully use and benefit from the transmission system.

letters.desc: Heron supports the ANOPR's co-located generation framework (Principle 3) as valuable but says it describes only one of several sound architectures. It asks the Commission to explicitly recognize energy-integrated power electronics as an equally valid reliability compliance pathway alongside co-located generation.
quotes: why energy-integrated power conversion, not only co-located generation, should be recognized as a valid compliance pathway for large load reliability requirements
The Commission should update its reliability compliance framework to explicitly recognize integrated power electronics solutions as a valid pathway alongside co-located generation.

letters.desc: LS Power supports incentivizing co-located generation and studying load and supply together. However, it firmly opposes ANOPR Principle 10's proposal to apply SSR/RMR-type analysis to existing generation serving co-located data center load, arguing this wrongly treats co-location as a partial suspension and discriminates against new large load.
quotes: It is critically important for the Commission to incent large load to bring its own generation (referred to in the Proposed ANOPR as "hybrid facilities"), and we urge the Commission to craft final rules with this in mind.

Large load interconnection rules should provide an expedited process for generation paired with co-located new large load. In order to qualify for expedited interconnection consideration, the large load must bring generation that matches its maximum capacity and energy needs.

The Commission should require that hybrid facility (large load and associated matching generation) interconnections with the interstate transmission grid be studied together where they are anticipated to interconnect electrically close to each other.
LS Power does not support this principle and supports the EPSA position on this principle.

EPSA rejects the underlying premise that existing generation that is moved behind the meter to serve data center load is akin to a partial suspension or otherwise warrants RMR/SSR type analysis for deactivating resources.
To introduce resource adequacy as a consideration in determining whether and at what cost to interconnect new large load would necessarily discriminate against that new load and existing generators.

letters.desc: The Maryland PSC supports co-location only with new, not existing, generation. It opposes partial suspension of existing generators to serve co-located load, finding that approach raises prices without solving the underlying supply shortfall. It also flags netting as a reliability and planning blind spot.
quotes: Bringing new (large) load on simultaneously with a matching amount of new generation/storage would maintain the supply/demand balance existing on the grid, thus causing minimal impact to the marginal cost of energy and capacity and lessening the need for network upgrades.

netting load against generation supply at hybrid facilities could pose a risk to grid reliability. Depending on how the hybrid arrangement is configured and how it is treated by system planners, netting load against the generator's supply to the grid may risk the load: (a) escaping the "view" of grid operators during normal operations; and (b) being excluded from future planning scenarios.

Existing generation currently serving customers should not be allowed to suspend their existing service, in whole or in part, simply to serve new large load. Such a suspension would have an adverse impact on cost and raise energy prices.

letters.desc: The MISO Transmission Owners accept that co-location arrangements need to be studied but insist they must stay within state law limits and require gross metering of load and generation to protect system reliability and cost-allocation integrity.
quotes: large load owners should only be able to co-locate and contract for power directly from generators to the extent state laws and regulations allow.  Second, it is critical to both system planning and operational awareness that load and generation are studied and metered separately, on a gross rather than a net basis.
the MISO Transmission Owners are concerned that the Eleventh and Twelfth Principles raise significant cost allocation concerns, as well as undue discrimination concerns

letters.desc: Missouri PSC supports studying co-located hybrid arrangements but warns that co-located generation costs must not fall on retail customers if the generation becomes unnecessary. States retain authority over the siting and approval of co-located generation.
quotes: The Missouri PSC supports efficient and comprehensive study procedures of hybrid facilities, but emphasizes that hybrid facility arrangements must be structured to prevent harm to the local utility and other customers.
Other customers should not bear the costs of co-located generation that becomes unnecessary if, for example, data centers become more efficient over time.

letters.desc: NRECA supports requiring control facilities at co-located sites to prevent unauthorized grid use, but warns that reliability studies alone are insufficient. Market-power studies and possible RTO rule changes are needed to address competitive risks from load co-located with existing generation.
quotes: hybrid interconnections should be required to install system protection and control facilities to prevent unauthorized injections or withdrawals that exceed the respective rights (e.g., leaning on the transmission system when co-located generation is not adequate to meet the large load's need).

Such control facilities are necessary not only for reliability purposes, but also to prevent market disruptions and manipulation arising from unauthorized injections or withdrawals, including the marketing of excess power unneeded to serve the hybrid load.
Additional, specific market-power studies will be necessary for these purposes in RTO/ISO regions with organized electric markets. Modifications of RTO/ISO market rules may be necessary.

letters.org: Natural Resource Defense CouncilSustainable FERC ProjectClean Air Task Force ,Coalition for Affordable Utility Services and Energy Efficie ,EARTHJUSTICE ,ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENSE FUND ,MONTANA ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION CENTER ,Sierra Club ,Southern Environmental Law Center ,
letters.desc: The filers support studying large loads together with co-located generation and favor physical control technologies over financial penalties to enforce injection and withdrawal limits. They flag, however, that co-location with existing generators can worsen market power incentives and market manipulation risks that FERC must address.
quotes: Control technologies are a better approach because they can allow direct control of injections or withdrawals and thus prevent any harm associated with unauthorized actions, such as distortions in market prices or threats to reliability.

co-location arrangements involving existing generators can heighten the concern with deficiencies in market power mitigation rules by exacerbating certain market participants' incentives to abuse market power and engage in market manipulation.

letters.desc: ODEC supports allowing hybrid and co-located large load configurations but argues they require strict cost and reliability scrutiny. The filing warns that partial or full suspension of existing generators to serve co-located loads siphons resources from customers who funded those generators, and calls for must-run studies in those cases. ODEC also requires that hybrid configuration loads bear all costs they cause.
quotes: "Swift" and "diligent" are not mutually exclusive, and the Commission can – and should – issue a reasoned decision that will provide large loads a way to interconnect with the transmission system and/or through hybrid configurations, in a manner that preserves reliability and resource adequacy, and at rates that are just, reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.

the Final Rule should recognize that interconnecting large loads that will result in partial or full suspension of an existing resource raises different and more concerning impacts than a load interconnection with a build-your-own generation arrangement that includes new generation.
The former arrangement will siphon resources away from the very loads that have financially supported the existing generation, at a time when resource adequacy is already severely threatened.

ODEC supports the ANOPR proposal in Principle 10, to require a system support resource/reliability must run type study for partial suspension of existing generators to serve new loads at the same location.
the Commission must also require measures to ensure that large loads in hybrid configurations are responsible for all of the costs caused by their interconnection.

letters.desc: OMS appreciates incentives for co-located generation as a way to reduce upgrade costs and protect existing customers, but calls for stringent rules ensuring co-located and flexible loads pay for all grid services and do not shift costs onto ratepayers.
quotes: FERC should confirm that interconnection under this framework does not confer a right to self-procure from wholesale markets, except through approved arrangements such as co-location or behind-the-meter generation used for flexibility or demand-response purposes.
enabling load flexibility is critical to accelerating the interconnection of large loads while maintaining a reliable and affordable grid for existing customers.

as the Commission develops proposed requirements for flexible or co-located loads, it should ensure potential changes to existing regulatory constructs, public engagement processes, cost allocation frameworks, wholesale markets, and transmission planning are sufficiently stringent to shield existing customers from negative impacts and to determine whether the large loads are paying for the grid services they use (transmission, ancillary services, reliability backstop, etc.).

letters.desc: The PA PUC opposes the ANOPR's broad co-location and hybrid rules as part of an overbroad package, but acknowledges that guidance limited strictly to hybrid load-plus-generation at the same point of interconnection may be permissible and beneficial if it shortens study timelines.
quotes: The recommendations that (1) load and hybrid facilities be studied together with generating facilities for efficient siting and be subject to standardized study deposits, readiness requirements, and withdrawal penalties; (2) hybrid facilities be studied based on the amount of injection and/or withdrawal rights requested to provide incentives for co-location with new generation facilities; (3) any hybrid interconnection install the system protection facilities necessary to prevent unauthorized injections or withdrawals that exceed the respective rights; (4) financial penalties for load facilities and hybrid facilities; (5) expedited consideration of interconnection studies of large loads and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable and dispatchable; and (6) that load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that are assigned through the interconnection studies all have widespread economic and political ramifications.
However, if limited to hybrid interconnections of load and generation at the same point-of-interconnection, there may be greater room for discussion.

Further guidance on paired interconnection studies could be welcome, subject to a more detailed proposed rule and opportunity for comment, if that guidance minimized the need for transmission buildout and interconnection study timelines due to the nature of that paired interconnection.

letters.desc: Shell Energy supports co-location and hybrid study approaches for faster siting but wants clarity on resource adequacy treatment, transmission rights, and ancillary service obligations. The co-location model should be an option, not a permanent operating requirement.
quotes: Shell Energy believes hybrid/co-located load and generation facilities should retain the right to request future study and full market participation without system protection facilities or system protection schemes limiting injection and withdrawal to low net MW values, where full grid access better suits their long-run operational needs, or after necessary network upgrades enter service.

Shell Energy supports analyzing the net impact of hybrid/co-located load with generation to allow for more efficient siting, faster study processing and shorter transmission infrastructure construction timelines.

In regions where generators must own firm transmission rights to be eligible to sell resource adequacy, this rulemaking should clarify that generation resources are eligible to sell capacity or resource adequacy products to co-located load without requiring firm transmission rights.

Shell Energy supports that principle 10 provides a transparency mechanism into bilateral transactions to serve large loads. Competitive markets require transparency so that shifts in underlying market fundamentals can be reflected in prices to signal and incentivize investment where needed.

letters.desc: AEMA opposes proposals from PJM IMM and EPSA that would require new large loads to pair with new generation as a precondition for expedited interconnection. Generation matching should be one optional pathway among several, evaluated on a technology-neutral basis alongside storage, software, and other demand-side tools.
quotes: AEMA strongly urges the Commission to reject arguments from the Independent Market Monitor for PJM ("PJM IMM"), the Electric Power Supply Association ("EPSA"), the Illinois Attorney General, and others suggesting that large loads must "bring their own generation" or that demand-side solutions are inferior to generation assets.

Mandating that every new large load be paired with new generation forces the construction of redundant capital assets when cost-effective flexibility could otherwise allow that load to be served by the existing system. This approach would unnecessarily inflate the cost of AI infrastructure and add years of supply chain backlog.
AEMA urges the Commission to treat generation matching as one optional pathway among many to achieve flexibility, not as a mandatory precondition for timely interconnection.

a final rule singling out loads or hybrid facilities that pair matching generation as the sole mechanism for expedited interconnection—while excluding verifiable load flexibility—would be unduly discriminatory.

letters.desc: The Alliance warns that co-location queue preferences create a market tilted toward well-capitalized private developers and against Tribal sovereign developers. It asks the Commission to confine the net withdrawal/injection rule to a calculation tool, not a queue-priority mechanism.
quotes: Prioritizing large load interconnection applicants in the queue based on whether they are co-located with generation creates a market where hybrid facilities may be more competitive than non-hybrid facilities.

We call on the Commission to clarify that this proposed rule only allows the calculation of net withdrawal/injection rights and does not impact the order of prioritization in the interconnection queue.

letters.desc: The filer characterizes developer-owned behind-the-meter gas plants colocated with data centers as expensive and risky, framing them as an untenable workaround that grid-based flexible interconnection should replace.
quotes: To secure power more quickly, data-center developers are increasingly resorting to expensive, risky solutions such as building and operating their own behind-the-meter natural gas power plants colocated with large datacenter campuses.

letters.desc: EEI opposes cost allocation based on net injection or withdrawal for co-located and hybrid facilities. Because the generation component can go offline and the full load then depends on the broader transmission system, netting understates actual system reliance and creates cost shifts to other customers similar to problematic state net metering programs.
quotes: Adopting a default rule that allocates the costs of transmission service for co-located or hybrid large loads based on net injection/withdrawal rights will create adverse cost impacts for other customers and is not necessary to achieve the goals of the DOE ANOPR.

the entire arrangement is connected to and reliant on the broader system.  As one example, there is a possibility that the generation component of a hybrid facility becomes unavailable, and the full load (i.e., without netting) looks to non-co-located resources to be served.
EEI's recommended approach--a default cost-allocation rule based on gross load for both transmission service and ancillary services--is the measured, most consumer-protective approach.

letters.desc: EPSA rejects applying RMR or SSR analysis to generation moved behind the meter to serve data center load. It argues that reliability assessments for co-located or hybrid arrangements must be limited to safe interconnection, and that introducing resource adequacy criteria would discriminate against new loads and existing generators.
quotes: EPSA rejects the underlying premise that existing generation that is moved behind the meter to serve data center load is akin to a partial suspension or otherwise warrants RMR/SSR type analysis for deactivating resources.
Any reliability assessment for co-located or hybrid arrangements must be limited to whether and how the proposed new load can be reliably and safely interconnected to the grid.
To introduce resource adequacy as a consideration in determining whether and at what cost to interconnect new large load would necessarily discriminate against that new load and existing generators.

letters.desc: Entergy opposes the proposed net-basis treatment for co-located hybrid facilities, arguing it is too simplistic and will leave real injection and withdrawal risks unidentified, threatening grid reliability.
quotes: It would be overly simplistic to assume that a hybrid load's net injection or withdrawal impacts on the grid will be constant over any period of time.  Reliability issues can arise if a study of a hybrid facility assumes a certain level of energy injections onto the grid, but injections in fact exceed that level, or if no withdrawal rights are assumed but withdrawals occur.

netting should not affect the way an interconnection request is studied.  Studying hybrid facilities in the manner contemplated by the proposed ANOPR may fail to identify needed network upgrades, because it will be blind to potentially substantial new loads, as long as those new loads are 'hybrid.'

letters.desc: Expedited large load interconnection could compromise grid reliability by delaying connections for other resources. The potential reliability gains from data center flexibility should not outweigh the risks of deprioritizing additional grid resources.
quotes: fast tracking data center interconnections at the expense of connecting new resources to the grid could lead to reliability issues that outstrip the benefits flexibility can provide.

letters.desc: Maven argues that LCEP is structured as a co-location product that advantages existing generator owners: the incumbent's consent becomes the price of speed, giving it bargaining power in site deals, power purchase agreements, and tolling structures. Smaller generators and independent developers cannot replicate this advantage because they do not own the Points of Interconnection.
quotes: a tariff-enabled mechanism to convert incumbent control of existing generation Points of Interconnection into a gatekeeping product for the nation's fastest-growing source of electricity demand
the owner of an existing generation Point of Interconnection would control who gets expedited access to the transmission system for large-load interconnection
The consent requirement is not a procedural formality. It is the mechanism through which the incumbent monetizes its bottleneck position.

letters.desc: The filer rejects Principles 11 and 12 as applied to co-located load and generation, asserting that charging only for net grid impact fails to capture the real transmission benefits co-located loads receive and would shift costs to other ratepayers.
quotes: Maintaining the status quo of cost responsibility for transmission service and ancillary services will provide large load owners and transmission providers clarity and certainty and avoid preventable and unnecessary litigation.

Basing load owners' transmission service responsibilities on their withdrawal rights alone fails to account for transmission service large load owners will use during the planned and unplanned outages that generators experience, i.e., times when large load owners will benefit from the broader transmission system.

letters.desc: The Market Monitor opposes the narrow co-location model under which existing generators withdraw from PJM capacity markets to serve behind-the-meter data center load. This shifts reliability risk and costs to all other PJM customers, is inconsistent with just and reasonable rates, and could undermine the entire PJM market structure.
quotes: Co-located load is simply a way to wish away the reliability issue and more importantly to undermine the PJM markets and impose unacceptably large reliability and monetary costs on all other PJM customers.

The Commission should reject the co-location option as inconsistent with PJM's competitive markets, inconsistent with just and reasonable rates, and inconsistent with the goal of the ANOPR to ensure the timely and orderly interconnection of large loads.

The narrowly defined co-location model that is the subject of Constellation's Complaint and Constellation's ongoing comments in the PJM CIFP process would allow existing generation to sell to a large new data center load and withdraw from the PJM capacity market. If allowed, this option could lead to the end of PJM markets.

letters.desc: ODEC warns that co-located generation at hybrid facilities must not be used to reduce interconnection cost responsibility or to avoid full transmission studies. It opposes merchant generators reclassifying deactivated capacity as new generation to win data-center supply contracts.
quotes: Generators experience both planned and unplanned outages; thus, the transmission facilities must be evaluated with only the load operational, not the generation.

ODEC does not support studying hybrid facilities based on the injection/withdrawal rights requested because we believe it will cause issues stemming from generator outages and the retirement of load or generating facilities, as the transmission system will still need to be built to accommodate either the load or the generating facility operating independently in the future.

This should not include any existing generators that deactivate all or part of their capacity to execute more lucrative large-load bilateral supply contracts with large loads that possess unlimited financial resources.

Facilities served by dedicated generation and hybrid facilities should be responsible for contributing to the upkeep and maintenance of the transmission system based on peak demand, without consideration of any co-located generation facilities.

letters.desc: PFT urges FERC to examine whether co-located loads are avoiding their fair share of grid upgrade costs. The DOE framing that bundles transmission interconnection with energy and capacity access could let co-located facilities argue entitlement to wholesale market services while escaping transmission charges.
quotes: Such arrangements potentially avoid transmission upgrade costs and network service charges while creating reliability concerns: largest customers that can satisfy their demand close to the point of generation, effectively reducing the pool of generation available to all other customers participating in markets.

DOE's assertion that transmission service encompasses 'the appurtenant benefits of such' threatens state jurisdiction to the extent that new large loads could, for example, argue that failure to provide them energy and capacity is a violation of the terms of their interconnection or entitles them to direct access to wholesale markets.

PFT urges FERC to support the existing functions of state utility regulators while focusing on reforming capacity markets, strengthening transmission planning requirements, and taking a hard look at whether co-located loads are avoiding their share of grid costs and upgrades.

letters.desc: Talen opposes the PJM Market Monitor's bring-your-own-generation proposal and any authority for RTOs to deny or condition load interconnection on self-supplied generation, arguing it conflicts with open-access principles and creates a two-tiered load system.
quotes: Proposals that require new large load customers to bring their own new generation are discriminatory.

Conditioning customer interconnections on BYOG or instructing PJM to deny service conflicts with bedrock open-access principles FERC established in Order No. 888 and Order No. 2000, which mandate non-discriminatory transmission service under a Commission-approved tariff.
FERC should reject any proposal that allows PJM (or any other RTO/ISO) to deny interconnection or prioritize BYOG arrangements.

letters.org: Utility Intervention Unit, New York State Department of Stat
letters.desc: The UIU opposes reduced interconnection requirements for co-located generation and load. Failing to study hybrid facilities for their full injection and withdrawal rights creates unnecessary reliability risks and queue distortions.
quotes: UIU opposes the contention that the hybrid facilities should not be required to meet the minimum interconnection requirements applicable to its entire load or generation.

The type of incentive promulgated in the ANOPR would distort queue prioritization, potentially allowing large loads to leapfrog generation projects competing for the same transfer capability because they are not required to financially support their full interconnection request.

letters.org: Wisconsin Electric Power CompanyWisconsin Public Service Corporation
letters.desc: WEC contends that co-located generation selling power to an adjacent large load is a retail sale, putting FERC regulation of that arrangement beyond its lawful authority. They ask any rule to bar co-located generators from serving load in violation of state retail franchise laws.
quotes: A generation facility that is co-located with a large load and which then sells its energy product to that load is, by definition, making a retail sale.  This is true regardless of whether the co-located load is interconnected at the transmission level or at distribution voltage.  Commission regulation of this retail sale would extend far beyond regulating interconnections as a "component" or "element" of transmission service and would clearly be ultra vires.

the Commission should make the "gross" amount of load the default approach for studying large load interconnections consistent with existing Commission precedent.  This will ensure that co-located arrangements are appropriately studied based on their actual use of the transmission system, even if the load or generation has its withdrawal or injection rights based on the net capacity behind the meter.

If the net withdrawal or injection of co-located facilities are permitted to influence transmission cost allocation, the Commission should ensure that there are adequate restrictions on the ability of the load or generation facility to withdraw or inject beyond their respective entitlements.

any rulemaking should ensure that franchised service territories are protected and that any processes mandated by a rule does not permit generators to serve co-located load in violation of retail franchise laws.

letters.desc: APS seeks clarification on utility backup obligations and risk allocation when large loads co-locate with generators.
quotes: Is the utility expected to back up all, some, or none of the load for a large load that is co-locating with a generator?

letters.desc: Equinix emphasizes that colocation and edge data centers, unlike hyperscale AI training facilities, must be located near dense urban load centers and cannot easily incorporate on-site generation. Rules that disadvantage these geographically constrained facilities would harm national security and financial sector interests.
quotes: data centers and their business models are highly heterogenous, serve different roles in our economy and national welfare, and have differing needs and capabilities with respect to their interactions with the energy system.
the vast majority of data centers, such as colocation and edge data centers, must be located as close to the businesses and public entities that they serve as possible.

it is not clear to us why the flexibility that could clearly offer our energy system such great benefit must, or even should, be either incorporated into the large load itself or necessarily located behind the same interconnection.

Those data centers located in dense metropolitan areas should be able to tap into the wealth of flexibility opportunities that surround them, creating a mutual benefit for those commercial, industrial or even residential users that could receive enhanced energy equipment or could easily absorb curtailment at a much lower economic and performance cost.

Penalizing those large loads that, for national security, financial sector or other reasons must maintain extremely high up-time, and for those same reasons are geographically constrained to areas that have limited ability to incorporate backup or co-located generation, would be contrary to national interests.

letters.desc: The filer describes how PJM identified multiple co-location options with distinct grid impacts, and how Irish rules distinguish proximity requirements for capacity obligations versus renewable energy targets. It presents these as reference points for regulators rather than advocating a particular model.
quotes: However, the American network operator, PJM, reveals several complications in its May 2025 publication, showing 8 options for large load co-location, identifying unique grid impacts of each.

CRU does not allow a data centre to meet its capacity obligation using remote generation elsewhere in Ireland. However, it does allow remote renewable generation to count toward the 80% renewable requirement.

letters.desc: WIRES flags that co-located load arrangements face cost shift dynamics similar to standalone large loads, because co-located customers may also escape NITS charges after paying network upgrade costs, leaving embedded system costs to other ratepayers.
quotes: cost responsibilities for co-located load arrangements bear similarities to the scenarios discussed above, with similar cost shift concerns.
